title: DBMS and SQL
description: Relational databases: keys, ER modelling, SQL queries, joins, aggregation, normalisation, transactions and indexing.

questions.prompt: What does DBMS stand for?
questions.explanation: A DBMS is software that stores, manages and retrieves data.

questions.prompt: Which language is used to query relational databases?
questions.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard relational query language.

questions.prompt: Which SQL command category does CREATE TABLE belong to?
questions.explanation: CREATE, ALTER and DROP are Data Definition Language commands.

questions.prompt: Which constraint uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL?
questions.explanation: A primary key is unique and not null for every row.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key do?
choices: References a key in another table
questions.explanation: A foreign key links rows to a primary or candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

questions.prompt: In an ER diagram, entities are conventionally drawn as what shape?
questions.explanation: Entities are rectangles, attributes ovals and relationships diamonds.

questions.prompt: Students enrol in many courses and each course has many students. What kind of relationship is this?
questions.explanation: Both sides can relate to many rows on the other side, which is many-to-many and needs a junction table.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which statement retrieves data from a table?
questions.explanation: SELECT reads rows from one or more tables.

questions.prompt: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a result?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each distinct combination once.

questions.prompt: Which clause sorts query results?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY sorts ascending by default; add DESC for descending.

questions.prompt: What does WHERE name LIKE 'A%' match?
questions.explanation: % matches any sequence of characters, so 'A%' means starts with A.

questions.prompt: Which join returns only rows with matching values in both tables?
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only rows where the join condition matches.

questions.prompt: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
choices: All rows of the left table plus matches from the right
All rows of the right table
questions.explanation: Unmatched left rows are kept, with NULLs for the right table's columns.

questions.prompt: A CROSS JOIN of tables with 3 and 4 rows returns how many rows?
questions.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs every row with every row: 3 x 4 = 12.

questions.prompt: Which join returns all rows from both tables, filling NULLs where there is no match?
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate function counts rows?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: HAVING applies conditions to aggregated groups.

questions.prompt: What does AVG(salary) ignore?
questions.explanation: Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) skip NULLs.

questions.prompt: A table is in first normal form (1NF) when:
choices: Every column holds atomic values with no repeating groups
Every determinant is a candidate key
questions.explanation: 1NF requires atomic values and no repeating groups.

questions.prompt: Second normal form (2NF) removes:
choices: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
questions.explanation: 2NF removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.

questions.prompt: Third normal form (3NF) removes:
choices: Transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on the key
questions.explanation: In 3NF non-key attributes depend only on the key, not on other non-key attributes.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of normalisation?
questions.explanation: Normalisation organises data to avoid duplication and anomalies.

questions.prompt: What does the A in ACID stand for?
questions.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction happens entirely or not at all.

questions.prompt: Which command makes a transaction's changes permanent?
questions.explanation: COMMIT makes the transaction's changes durable.

questions.prompt: What does ROLLBACK do?
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK discards uncommitted changes and restores the previous state.

questions.prompt: Which ACID property guarantees committed data survives a crash?
questions.explanation: Durability means committed changes persist even after failures.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of an index?
questions.explanation: Indexes let the database find rows without scanning the whole table.

questions.prompt: What is a downside of having too many indexes?
choices: Slower INSERT and UPDATE and more storage
questions.explanation: Every write must also update each index, and indexes take space.

questions.prompt: Which data structure do most relational database indexes use?
questions.explanation: B-trees keep keys sorted and shallow, giving logarithmic lookups with few disk reads.

lessons.title: What is a DBMS?
lessons.body: A database management system stores, organises and retrieves data. In a relational database, data lives in tables made of rows (records) and columns (attributes), described by a schema. SQL is the language used to define and query data.

lessons.title: SQL command categories
lessons.body: DDL defines structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP). DML manipulates data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT). DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE). TCL manages transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
lessons.example:
CREATE TABLE student (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO student VALUES (1, 'Asha');

lessons.title: Keys and constraints
lessons.body: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. A candidate key is any column set that could serve as the primary key. A foreign key references a key in another table and enforces referential integrity. Other constraints include UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT.

lessons.title: ER modelling and relationships
lessons.body: An ER diagram shows entities (rectangles), attributes (ovals) and relationships (diamonds). Cardinality can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is implemented with a junction table holding both foreign keys.

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
lessons.body: SELECT chooses columns, FROM names the table, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts (ASC by default) and DISTINCT removes duplicate rows. LIKE matches patterns where % is any sequence and _ is one character. LIMIT restricts the number of rows.
lessons.example:
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM student
WHERE name LIKE 'A%'
ORDER BY city;

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
lessons.body: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows and DELETE removes rows. Always include a WHERE clause with UPDATE and DELETE, otherwise every row is affected.
lessons.example:
UPDATE student SET city = 'Bengaluru' WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM student WHERE id = 2;

lessons.title: SQL joins
lessons.body: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right has no match. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image and FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both. CROSS JOIN produces every combination, so m and n rows give m x n.
lessons.example:
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM student s
INNER JOIN enrol e ON e.sid = s.id
INNER JOIN course c ON c.id = e.cid;

lessons.title: Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.body: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise rows. GROUP BY forms groups, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation while WHERE filters rows before it. Aggregates ignore NULLs, except COUNT(*) which counts rows.
lessons.example:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary)
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.body: A subquery is a query nested inside another. It can supply a value, a list for IN, or an existence test with EXISTS. A correlated subquery refers to columns of the outer query and runs per outer row.
lessons.example:
SELECT name FROM student
WHERE id IN (SELECT sid FROM enrol);

lessons.title: Normalisation: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
lessons.body: Normalisation reduces redundancy and update anomalies. 1NF: atomic values and no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the key. BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key.

lessons.title: Transactions and ACID
lessons.body: A transaction is a unit of work. ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and Durability (committed data survives crashes). COMMIT saves changes and ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted ones.

lessons.title: Indexes
lessons.body: An index is an auxiliary structure, usually a B-tree or B+ tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table, speeding up reads. Each index slows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and uses storage, so index the columns you filter, join and sort on, not everything.
